Training your eye. That's what it boils down to. Many trials, many errors. It's just going to take time. So! Give yourself a break from time to time, the subconscious works in mysterious ways. Another way you can learn is to try trading without a stop (put an OH shit! stop for safety) for a while and exit manually where you would normally put your stop. This forces you to continue thinking about the market reaction at your predefined level and proactively make a decision on when to exit, when to hold, when to move your stop back in. It buys you time to think about what price is doing, observe HTF, observe correlations, what you might have missed, where it might be targeting, where else it could reverse, why you should or shouldn't stay in the trade and accept the bigger risk.

When you get it wrong and price blows straight through, that usually means you have missed one or two things completely. I've got a growing checklist that fires off in my mind when I'm observing charts, placing trades, deciding what to do next...it only takes a few extra seconds to stop, breathe and think... Does it make sense in the HTF? Does it make sense in the LTF? Where is price coming from/going to in the HTF/LTF? What has price just done on approach? Broken a range? Broken some other FL I ignored? Flagged? Compressed? Finding support/resistance on new price action? Is there evidence of momentum at this level? Is the level even fresh? Time of day? News? Is TG1 far away enough to make this worthwhile? Any correlations to support the strength/weakness of the currency?

You're good at this. Find out the reason why something failed, make note in your head and move on.

p.s. Have you visited the Price is Everything thread on FF? I find myself going back there every other month to view Reds and Dropped Onions posts through the lens of my new understandings. Observe how they read price, its very iterative, in the moment, baby sitting the trade at every turn. It's a great way to learn to apply your thinking on top of theirs.

p.p.s. The trading without a stop suggestion is purely to get you out of the routine of setting and forgetting and into the zone of continuous decision making and understanding the reaction and if its meeting your expectation or not. You can worry about the R:R stuff after you feel confident that you're reading price correctly and consistently.

Thank you for the kind works pal, they mean a lot coming from you, I learned a lot from your journal.

I think the "no stop" suggestion is a really good one - I often find myself getting "price blindness" once a trade kicks in, and I will just ignore all the signs that it's going against me, and hold stubbornly even though I know I should be out of the thing. I guess if you've read your zone correctly then you can "trust the zone", but if you've got the wrong one, then holding blindly through PA going against you isn't going to do anything except get you stopped out!

Those are some great pointers, and I'm definitely trying to take all of those on board when I'm evaluating a trade. It's quite a lot to hold in your head at once, and I think as much as anything, that's what takes the real time to get good at - just holding so much information comfortably at once in your head. Just endless repetition until it becomes second nature.

I've not actually made it past the first 50 pages or so of PIE, it was a little daunting to be honest there's so much of it. I know there must be some great info in there, since it's where RTM originated. so I should set myself aside an hour or two a day and just get started ploughing through it.

New realisations are dawning on me daily at the moment as I become better at reading the interaction of important flags. I've noticed that there's a "key level" inside each flag, or at FTR edges - the precise place that the orders were dumped into the market. Once this key level goes, which is sometimes a DP only a few pips wide, the entire FL can be considered as dead. There was a comment by Yogi on the FF thread that put me on to this idea.

Putting in about 12-14 hours a day currently in front of charts, I think I'm getting a bit obsessed;-) I hate it when there's a puzzle I can't solve!

All the best pal

Hello, I still feel like risk:reward and probabilities don't get enough attention on this forum.

Here's a story (queue violin): when I first got interested in trading, probably much like some of you did, I created spreadsheets which linearly took my meager account deposit from rags to riches in a matter of 50 excel rows! As it turned out, I am not the kind of trader who can string together an infinite amount of wins in a row. So a while ago I created a pretty basic spreadsheet using excels Random number generator, which would model a simple equity curve a little closer to my reality. Stumbled across it again today, made it presentable, thought I would share it. Alternatively, there are also a multitude of modelers when you google equity curve generators.

Discipline and patience; something I struggled with from the beginning and still do to some extent. Having something visual, whether it be a trading plan, wallpaper of an expensive car or house or a sexy randomised equity curve helps to remind me that this is a long term game, and that it is actually okay to be WRONG, and have a string of losses, and the importance of getting over losses quickly. It really is amazing what IRON DISCIPLINE will achieve.

Food for thought: How long would it realistically take you to execute 1,000 quality trades, and what could your equity curve look like after that type of sample size?
